title: If You Build a House Right on the Dirt...
sources: JLC 'Foundation Footing Fundamentals' / Wikipedia 'Shallow foundation' / GreenBuildingAdvisor 'All About Footings': soil compresses and settles under a building's load; a footing is wider than the wall so it spreads the load over more soil
FEMA EMI IS-280 'Allowable Bearing Capacity' / engineerfix 'What Is a Spread Footing': spreading the same weight over a larger area lowers the pressure on the soil (the snowshoe principle)
Fine Homebuilding 'How it Works: Frost Heave' / Wikipedia 'Frost heaving' / NRC Canadian Building Digest 128: water in soil freezes into ice lenses that grow and push the ground and footings upward
Iowa DNR 'Why does water expand when it freezes' / IAPWS (via InspectAPedia): water expands roughly nine percent as it freezes

IRC R403.1.4 (ICC; WAC 51-51-0403) and Minnesota Rule 1303.1600 'Footing depth for frost protection' (MN Revisor, Cornell LII): footings must sit below the frost line; Minnesota requires 42 inches in the south and 60 inches (five feet) in the northern zone

Practical Engineering 'Why does concrete need reinforcement' / Explain That Stuff 'Concrete and reinforced concrete' / Ask the Builder 'Reinforcing Steel in Footings': concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension, so steel rebar is cast inside

FEMA hurricane building-performance reports / DOE BASC 'Continuous load path failure due to improper connections between home and its foundation' / AWC + IRC R403.1.6: houses not anchored can slide off foundations; anchor bolts set in the concrete hold the wooden sill plate down

lines.text: If you build a house right on the dirt, it slowly sinks.
lines.caps: If you build a house | right on the dirt, | it slowly sinks.

lines.text: Because soil gets squeezed under all that weight.
lines.caps: Because soil gets squeezed | under all that weight.

lines.text: So, builders dig a trench, and pour a wide concrete footing.
lines.caps: So, builders dig a trench, | and pour a wide | concrete footing.

lines.text: It spreads the weight out, like snowshoes on snow.
lines.caps: It spreads the weight out, | like snowshoes on snow.

lines.text: But in winter, the water in the soil freezes, and grows.
lines.caps: But in winter, | the water in the soil | freezes, and grows.

lines.text: That ice pushes the ground up, and cracks the walls. It's called frost heave.
lines.caps: That ice pushes | the ground up, | and cracks the walls. | It's called frost heave.

lines.text: So, footings go below the frost line, where the ground never freezes.
lines.caps: So, footings go | below the frost line, | where the ground | never freezes.

lines.text: In northern Minnesota, that's five feet down.
lines.caps: In northern Minnesota, | that's 5 feet down.

lines.text: But concrete cracks easily when it bends.
lines.caps: But concrete | cracks easily | when it bends.

lines.text: So, steel bars called rebar go inside, and hold it together.
lines.caps: So, steel bars | called rebar go inside, | and hold it together.

lines.text: And a strong storm can shove a wooden house right off its base.
lines.caps: And a strong storm | can shove a wooden house | right off its base.

lines.text: So, steel bolts are set in the wet concrete, to tie the walls down.
lines.caps: So, steel bolts | are set in the wet concrete, | to tie the walls down.

lines.text: You see, the ground isn't solid. It squeezes, freezes and moves.
lines.caps: You see, | the ground isn't solid. | It squeezes, | freezes and moves.

lines.text: That's why every house stands on a hidden concrete foot.
lines.caps: That's why every house | stands on a hidden | concrete foot.
